column3: In consistent hashing, the largest hash value wraps around to the smallest hash value (`paper-dynamo-columns#p10`).
Each node in the system is assigned a random value within the ring space which represents its “position” on the ring (`paper-dynamo-columns#p10`).

Each data item identified by a key is assigned to a node by hashing the data item’s key to yield its position on the ring, and then walking the ring clockwise to find the first node with a position larger than the item’s position (`paper-dynamo-columns#p10`).
Each node becomes responsible for the region in the ring between it and its predecessor node on the ring (`paper-dynamo-columns#p11`).
In consistent hashing, a key belongs to the first node found by walking the ring clockwise from the key's position, and each node is responsible for the region between it and its predecessor.
According to the ScyllaDB documentation, partitioning data by a partition key makes a lookup by that key efficient, while finding a row by a non-partition key needs a full table scan.
A global secondary index lets ScyllaDB search efficiently on a non-partition column.

ScyllaDB makes its secondary indexes global rather than local because the size of an index is proportional to the size of the indexed data, and storing the whole index on a single node would limit it to the capacity of one node.

According to the same documentation, a global index is a materialized view that has the indexed column as its partition key, and a read can use the value of the indexed column to find the matching index table row in the cluster.
The documentation notes that writes are slower than with local indexing because of the overhead of keeping the indexed view up to date.
